DEPARTMENT SEP LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 24NWCV03031    Hearing Date: September 22, 2026    Dept: SEP

DELUX DESIGN & CONSTRUCTION, INC. v. MANNAVA, ET AL. 

CASE NO.:  24NWCV03031 

HEARING: 09/22/2026 @ 9:30 AM 

 

#10 

TENTATIVE ORDER 

 

Defendants Ravi Mannava and Anuradha Srinivasan’s motion to expunge the mechanic’s lien is GRANTED. 

 

Moving party to give notice.  

 

Defendants Ravi Mannava and Anuradha Srinivasan (Defendants) move to expunge the mechanics lien recorded by Plaintiff Delux Design & Construction, Inc. (Plaintiff or Delux). 

 

Background 

 

On September 6, 2024, Plaintiff filed this breach of contract action against Defendants and Does 1 through 50. On October 2, 2025, Plaintiff filed the operative first amended complaint (FAC). The FAC alleges that in February of 2023, Plaintiff and Defendants entered into an oral contract for Plaintiff to provide the materials and installation for a first and second floor addition to 13349 Durango Place, Cerritos, California 90703 (Premises) consistent with certain plans (Project). (FAC, ¶ 7.) The FAC alleges that Defendants breached the agreement by failing to pay the balance due to Plaintiff. (FAC, ¶ 8.) The FAC asserts five causes of action: (1) Breach of Contract; (2) Quantum Meruit; (3) Open Book Account; (4) Account Stated; and (5) Foreclosure of Mechanics Lien. 

 

On September 11, 2024, Plaintiff filed a Notice of Lis Pendens as to the Premises. 

 

On June 11, 2025, Defendants filed a cross-complaint and on October 9, 2025, Defendants filed the operative first amended cross-complaint (FAXC) against Plaintiff, Glory Spring Construction Inc. (Glory Spring), Fan-Fu Tseng (Arthur), Fan Wen Tsen (Kent), Hudson Insurance Company, The Western Surety Company, and Roes 1 through 100. The FAXC alleges that Arthur misled Defendants into believing he was a representative of Glory Spring to induce Defendants to contract with Glory Spring for the Project, but Arthur was actually the RMO of Delux which did not have a CSLB license at all relevant times. (FAXC, ¶¶ 36-28.) The FAXC asserts ten causes of action: (1) Intentional Misrepresentation; (2) Negligent Misrepresentation; (3) Concealment; (4) Violation of Business & Professions Code, § 7031 (Disgorgement); (5) Violation of Business & Professions Code § 7159; (6) Breach of Contract; (7) Negligence; (8) Breach of Implied Covenant to Perform Work in a Good and Competent Manner; (9) Action to Expunge Mechanic’s Lien Civil Code § 3118; and (10) Action on Surety Bond Business & Professions Code § 7071. 

 

Legal Standard 

 

“A motion to remove a mechanic's lien is recognized as a device that allows the property owner to obtain speedy relief from an unjustified lien or a lien of an unjustified amount without waiting for trial on the action to foreclose the lien.” (Howard S. Wright Construction Co. v. Superior Court (2003) 106 Cal.App.4th 314, 318, citing Lambert v. Superior Court (1991) 228 Cal.App.3d 383.) “The inquiry upon such motion is likewise limited to the ‘probable validity’ of the lien.” (Ibid.) “However, unlike the grant of a motion to expunge the notice of lis pendens, the grant of a motion to remove a mechanic's lien is essentially a judgment on the underlying foreclosure action that no lien exists—a judgment that, upon recordation, removes the lien from the public records.” (Ibid.) 

 

Civil Code section 8460 provides that “[t]he claimant shall commence an action to enforce a lien within 90 days after recordation of the claim of lien.” (Civ. Code, § 8460, subd. (a).) “If the claimant does not commence an action to enforce the lien within that time, the claim of lien expires and is unenforceable.” (Civ. Code, § 8460, subd. (a).) “The owner of property or the owner of any interest in property subject to a claim of lien may petition the court for an order to release the property from the claim of lien if the claimant has not commenced an action to enforce the lien within the time provided in Section 8460.” (Civ. Code, § 8480, subd. (a).)   

 

“The lien claimant has the burden of establishing the validity of the lien, [citation] including that the labor, services and/or materials were actually used in the construction, the reasonable value of the work and/or materials, and the date of completion or cessation of work.” (Basic Modular Facilities, Inc. v. Ehsanipour (1999) 70 Cal.App.4th 1480, 1485.) 

 

Request for Judicial Notice 

 

Defendants request the Court takes judicial notice of the following:  

 

  1. Contractor’s State License Board License Detail and Personnel List for License # 869173, Glory Spring Construction Inc.; 

  1. November 25, 2024 California Secretary of State Statement of Information for Glory Spring; 

  1. Contractor’s State License Board License Detail and Personnel List for License # 1005579, Delux Design & Construction Inc.; 

  1. Contractor’s State License Board Personnel License List for Tseng, Fan-Fu, a/k/a Arthur 

 

Defendants’ request for judicial notice is GRANTED pursuant to Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (h). 

 

Evidentiary Objections 

 

Plaintiff makes twelve evidentiary objections to the declaration of Mannava. The Court rules as follows:  

 

OVERRULED: 1-12 

 

Discussion 

 

Defendants move to expunge the mechanic’s lien placed on the Premises in the amount of $170,186.43 on June 6, 2024. Defendants argue the mechanic’s lien is fraudulent and invalid on the following grounds: (1) Plaintiff was not a direct contractor and failed to property serve a preliminary notice; (2) Plaintiff engaged in unlicensed contracting; and (3) Plaintiff furnished no labor or materials for the Project as it was done by Glory Spring and Arthur individually. 

 

Direct Contractor & Preliminary Notice 

 

Defendants argue that Plaintiff did not give a proper preliminary notice to Defendants as required under Civil Code section 8200. 

 

Pursuant to Civil Code section 8200, subdivision (a), “before recording a lien claim…a claimant shall give preliminary notice to…(1) [t]he owner or reputed owner.” “Compliance with this section is a necessary prerequisite to the validity of a lien claim…under this title.” (Civ. Code, § 8200, subd. (c).) Whether Plaintiff has a direct contractual relationship with Defendants is relevant because the statute excepts “[a] claimant with a direct contractual relationship with an owner or reputed owner” from this requirement. (Civ. Code, § 8200, subd. (e)(2).) “The rationale for excepting those under direct contract with the owner from serving a preliminary notice is that ‘the owner is generally apprised of potential lien claims by those with whom he deals directly, whereas it is difficult for him to learn of potential liens by those not under direct contract. [Citation.]’” (Kim v. JF Enterprises (1996) 42 Cal.App.4th 849, 855.) 

 

Defendants contend that despite Plaintiff’s allegations regarding an oral contract, a home improvement work project for more than $500 must be in writing among other requirements. (Bus. & Prof. Code, 7159, subd. (b).) Defendants also put forth proposal documents for the Project bearing the Glory Spring letterhead with Arthur’s signature and documents showing permits were brought by Kent of Glory Spring. (Mannava Decl., Exhs. C, E.) Defendants show that a permit issued by the City of Cerritos listed Defendants as the owners and Glory Springs as the contractor. (O’Brien Decl., Exh. A.) Defendants show that Arthur directed payments to be made to “Tseng,” not Plaintiff. (Mannava Decl., ¶ 16, Exh. F.) Defendants contend that there was nothing to lead them to understand that Plaintiff was the actual contractor. Thus, Defendants argue that since Plaintiff cannot establish a direct contractual relationship with Defendants, it was required to give preliminary notice. Defendants assert that they were never served with a preliminary notice. (Mannava Decl., ¶ 25.)  

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that preliminary notice was not required because Defendants contracted with Plaintiff. Plaintiff submits a declaration of the responsible managing director (RMO) of Plaintiff, Arthur. (Tseng Decl., ¶ 1.) Arthur asserts that he met with and discussed the Project with Defendants in his capacity of RMO for Plaintiff. (Tseng Decl., ¶¶ 2-3.) Arthur asserts that Defendants “retained Glory Spring Construction for the architectural design of their home. The[sic] were advised by me that Delux Design & Construction, Inc. was the contractor that was doing the construction on the project.” (Tseng Decl., ¶ 4.) Plaintiff states that the proposal bearing the Glory Spring letterhead “was submitted in error has[sic] I had provided the amounts for the work that Delux Design & Construction, Inc. was proposing to provide and I advised them that this proposal was from Delux Design & Construction and not from Glory Spring Construction. After the proposal was submitted, I met with [Defendants] and I explained that the proposal had been sent by my nephew since my wife was undergoing chemotherapy when the proposal was submitted and that Delux Design & Construction was the contractor they were hiring.” (Tseng Decl., ¶ 5.) As to the checks, Arthur asserts that “[t]he 2 checks…payable to ‘Tseng’ were payments that I on behalf of Delux Design & Construction, Inc. directed [Defendants] to be made payable to ‘Tseng’ who is my son that received the checks because Delux Design & Construction, Inc. owed money to my son who is a doctor that had loaned money to Delux Design & Construction, Inc. money during Covid and this was to repay those sums.” (Tseng Decl., ¶ 10.) Additionally, the two checks paid to Kent “were directed to Tsen Kent because Delux Design & Development had borrowed money from my brother who directed me to have payments made to his son Kent Tsen.” (Tseng Decl., ¶ 11.) 

 

Plaintiff provides the preliminary notice that it served to Defendants. (Tseng Decl., Exh. 2; Mannava Decl., Exh. G.) The preliminary notice lists “LUMX INC” as the claimant and Plaintiff as the name of the firm who contracted for the purchase of labor and service and as the direct contractor. (Tseng Decl., Exh. 2; Mannava Decl., Exh. G.) 

 

In reply, Defendants argue that Arthur’s declaration is self-serving. Defendants also argue that the declaration shows at best that Plaintiff, Arthur, Kent, and Glory Spring operate their businesses interchangeably by mistakenly using the wrong letterheads, directing payments to each other, and pulling permits in each other’s names. Defendants emphasize that contractors are required to operate under their own license. (See Bus. & Prof. Code, § 7117.) 

 

Here, it is undisputed that Plaintiff did not give notice to Defendants, at issue is whether Plaintiff is excepted as a direct contractor. (Tseng Decl., Exh. 2; Mannava Decl., Exh. G.) “ ‘Direct contractor’ means a contractor that has a direct contractual relationship with an owner” and a “ ‘[d]irect contract’ means a contract between an owner and a direct contractor that provides for all or part of a work of improvement.” (Civ. Code, §§ 8016, 8018.) 

 

Notably, here, Plaintiff’s only evidence of an agreement between Plaintiff and Defendants was that after the proposal bearing Glory Spring’s letterhead was given to Defendants, “[Arthur] met with [Defendants] and…explained that the proposal had been sent by my nephew since my wife was undergoing chemotherapy when the proposal was submitted and that Delux Design & Construction was the contractor they were hiring to perform the construction they advised that they had approved the budget and agreed to hire Delux Design and Construction to perform the work and did perform the project. I advised [Defendants] that Glory Spring Construction, Inc. was only doing the architectural design of the project.” (Tseng Decl., ¶ 5.) Given that the permits issued by the City of Cerritos reflect only Glory Spring as the contractor, that all payments were to “Tseng” only, and the proposal itself depicts Glory Spring letterhead with Arthur’s name, the Court agrees that Plaintiff does not establish the probable validity of a direct contractual relationship with Defendants. The evidence shows that at most, Defendants made agreements with Arthur. The purpose behind the direct contracting exception does not support Plaintiff’s position if Defendants did not know they were contracting with Plaintiff. (See Kim, supra, 42 Cal.App.4th at p. 855.) Further, Plaintiff, with the burden on this motion, does not show that it made any efforts to correct any of the mistakes such as re-submitting documents with the proper letterhead or explaining to Defendants why Arthur directed payments to anywhere besides to Plaintiff.  

 

As Plaintiff does not establish by a preponderance of evidence a direct contract between Plaintiff, in its name, and Defendants, as property owners, the Court finds that removal of the lien is warranted on this ground. (Civ. Code, § 8200, subd. (c) [“Compliance with this section is a necessary prerequisite to the validity of a lien claim”].) 

 

License 

 

Defendants argue that even if Plaintiff shows that it has a direct contractual relationship with Defendants, it is barred from bringing this action and enforcing its mechanic’s lien under Business & Professions Code section 7031, subdivision (a). 

 

[N]o person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a contractor, may bring or maintain any action, or recover in law or equity in any action, in any court of this state for the collection of compensation for the performance of any act or contract where a license is required by this chapter without alleging that they were a duly licensed contractor at all times during the performance of that act or contract regardless of the merits of the cause of action brought by the person, except that this prohibition shall not apply to contractors who are each individually licensed under this chapter but who fail to comply with Section 7029. 

 

(Bus. & Prof. Code, § 7031, subd. (a).) “This prohibition applies to a contractor seeking to foreclose his or her mechanic's lien [citations] and thus, by extension, to an unlicensed contractor’s right to file a mechanic's lien.” (Slatkin v. White (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 963, 967-68.) “No license, regardless of type or classification, shall be transferable to any other person or entity under any circumstances.” (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 7075.1, subd. (a).) 

 

Defendants establish that Plaintiff’s license is in the name of “Delux Design & Construction Inc.” and thus does not permit Plaintiff to act under a different name. (RJN, Exh. 3.) Defendants establish that Arthur does not have an individual license. (RJN, Exhs. 3-4.) Further, Arthur is not an authorized personnel member of Glory Spring. (RJN, Exh. 1.) Thus, Defendants argue that Arthur either improperly acted under Glory Spring’s license or acted under his own individual capacity.  

 

Plaintiff does not address the licensing issues in its opposition. Plaintiff generally argues that the fact that Defendants are not disputing the amounts billed indicates that Defendants are avoiding paying for the services. In reply, Defendants interpret this as an unjust enrichment argument and respond that “[r]egardless of the equities, section 7031 bars all actions, however they are characterized, which effectively seek ‘compensation’ for illegal unlicensed contract work.” (Hydrotech Systems, Ltd. v. Oasis Waterpark (1991) 52 Cal.3d 988, 997.) “In a clear case even where ‘the defendant may be left in possession of some benefit he should in good conscience turn over to the plaintiff’ the importance of the public purpose in deterring the illegal conduct is deemed to outweigh the ‘unjust enrichment’ which enforcement of the statute entails.” (Jackson v. Pancake (1968) 266 Cal.App.2d 307, 310.) 

 

Here, the Court does not find that a preponderance of evidence supports removing the lien on this ground. The CSLB documents, without more, do not establish that Plaintiff performed unlicensed work as the documents do not show that Plaintiff was without a license at the relevant times. The confusion regarding the identities of the contracting parties does not necessarily reflect that unlicensed work was performed at this time. 

 

Labor and Materials 

 

Defendants lastly argue that Plaintiff cannot establish that it furnished the labor, services, or materials under the mechanic’s lien rather than someone else. Defendants argue that since the evidence only identifies Glory Spring or Arthur, Plaintiff cannot now claim a lien entitlement for work it did not perform under its own name. 

 

Here, Plaintiff does not actually produce any evidence supporting the reasonable value of its work and labor. Plaintiff does not delineate the costs of its work relative to the purported architectural design work performed by Glory Spring. “The lien claimant has the burden of establishing the validity of the lien, [citation] including that the labor, services and/or materials were actually used in the construction, the reasonable value of the work and/or materials, and the date of completion or cessation of work.” (Basic Modular Facilities, Inc. v. Ehsanipour (1999) 70 Cal.App.4th 1480, 1485.) 

 

Thus, the Court agrees that Plaintiff does not establish by a preponderance of evidence the amount that it paid for labor, services, or materials. 

 

Defendants’ motion to expunge the mechanic’s lien is GRANTED. 

 

Attorney’s Fees 

 

Defendants request attorney’s fees pursuant to Civil Code section 8488, subdivision (c). 

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that Civil Code section 8488 does not apply to this motion because Defendants did not move under Civil Code Section 8482.  

 

In reply, Defendants argue that “[a]lthough that subdivision appears in the article governing formal release-order petitions for expired liens (Civ. Code § 8482 et seq.), the Legislature’s clear policy is that the party who successfully removes an improper lien should not be forced to bear the cost of doing so.” (Reply, 8:5-8.)  

 

Here, Defendants bring a Lambert motion rather than a statutory petition to release a mechanic’s lien. Neither Lambert nor Howard articulate a basis for attorney’s fees. (See, gen., Howard S. Wright Construction Co., supra, 106 Cal.App.4th at p. 318; Lambert, supra, 228 Cal.App.3d at p. 383.) Civil Code section 8488 is based on specific procedural requirements under Civil Code section 8480, et seq. Defendants do not cite to authority for the alleged clear policy by the legislature regarding attorney’s fees. As Defendants do not articulate a proper statutory, judicial, or contractual basis for attorney’s fees, the Court declines to award them at this time. 

 

Accordingly, Defendants’ request for attorney’s fees is DENIED. 

Case Number: 25NWCV02310¿    Hearing Date: September 22, 2026    Dept: SEP

MEDINA v. O’NEILL, ET AL. 

CASE NO.: 25NWCV02310¿  

HEARING: 09/22/2026 @ 9:30 AM 

 

#11 

TENTATIVE ORDER 

 

Plaintiff Nicole Medina’s motion to quash deposition subpoenas is DENIED without prejudice. 

 

Moving party to give notice.  

 

Plaintiff Nicole Medina (Plaintiff) moves to quash or, alternatively, modify certain deposition subpoenas. 

 

Background 

 

On June 26, 2025, Plaintiff filed this personal injury action against Defendants Ronan O’Neill, Blanca Valle, and Does 1 through 25 (collectively, Defendants). The form complaint alleges that on June 29, 2023, at i-5 Southbound, 500 feet north of Tweedy Ave in the City of Norwalk, Plaintiff sustained injuries after she was first rear-ended by O’Neill and then faced a successive impact by Valle who was driving behind O’Neill. The complaint asserts two causes of action: (1) motor vehicle and (2) general negligence. 

 

On October 6, 2025, Plaintiff filed an Amendment to Complaint naming Jhony E. Fuentes as Doe 1. 

 

Legal Standard 

 

Under Code of Civil Procedure section 1985.3 subd. (g), a consumer whose personal records are sought by a subpoena duces tecum may bring a motion to quash or modify the subpoena five days prior to the date of production.  

 

Code of Civil Procedure section 1987.1 states the following:¿ 

 

“(a) If a subpoena requires the attendance of a witness or the production of books, documents, electronically stored information, or other things before a court, or at the trial of an issue therein, or at the taking of a deposition, the court, upon motion reasonably made by any person described in subdivision (b), or upon the court’s own motion after giving counsel notice and an opportunity to be heard, may make an order quashing the subpoena entirely, modifying it, or directing compliance with it upon those terms or conditions as the court shall declare, including protective orders. In addition, the court may make any other order as may be appropriate to protect the person from unreasonable or oppressive demands, including unreasonable violations of the right of privacy of the person.”  

 

For discovery purposes, information is relevant if it might reasonably lead to admissible evidence or might reasonably assist a party in evaluating the case, preparing for trial, or facilitating settlement. (Gonzalez v. Superior Court (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 1539, 1546; see Code Civ. Proc., § 2017.010 [“[a]ny party may obtain discovery regarding any matter, not privileged, that is relevant to the subject matter involved in the pending action or to the determination of any motion made in that action, if the matter either is itself admissible in evidence or appears reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence.”].) The rules are applied liberally in favor of permitting discovery. (Gonzalez, supra, 33 Cal.App.4th at p. 1546.) 

 

Pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 2025.420, subdivision (a): “Before, during, or after a deposition, any party, any deponent, or any other affected natural person or organization may promptly move for a protective order. The motion shall be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under Section 2016.040.” 

 

Discussion 

 

Plaintiff moves to quash multiple deposition subpoenas for production of business records issued by Defendants and “directed to PIH Health Whittier Hospital Human Resources, PIH Health Whittier Hospital Health Information Management Department, PIH Health Whittier Hospital Medical Records, and…additional custodians.” (Perez Decl., ¶ 5.) 

 

Procedural Deficiencies 

 

This motion must be denied on procedural grounds. 

 

First, as argued by Defendants in opposition, Plaintiff’s motion is untimely. Defendants contend that Plaintiff filed this motion 114 days after the April 14, 2026 production date and 108 days after the April 20, 2026 production date. 

 

“Any consumer whose personal records are sought by a subpoena duces tecum and who is a party to the civil action in which this subpoena duces tecum is served may, prior to the date for production, bring a motion under Section 1987.1 to quash or modify the subpoena duces tecum. Notice of the bringing of that motion shall be given to the witness and deposition officer at least five days prior to production.” (Code Civ. Proc., 1985.3, subd. (g).) While the Court does not deny this motion on this basis alone, the Court agrees that based on the production dates put forth by Defendants, this motion is untimely. (See Slagle v. Superior Court (1989) 211 Cal.App.3d 1309, 1312 [deadline is not jurisdictional].) 

 

Next, Plaintiff failed to put forth the actual deposition subpoenas. This is significant given that this motion seeks review of multiple deposition subpoenas to an unknown amount of entities. While Plaintiff contends the deposition subpoenas are attached to Plaintiff’s counsel’s declaration, there are no attached exhibits. (See Perez Decl., ¶ 6.) 

 

Further, on top of failing to attach the deposition subpoenas, Plaintiff did not originally provide separate statements. A separate statement is required for a motion to quash the production of documents or things at a deposition. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1345(a)(5).) Therefore, the Court did not have access to the deposition subpoenas themselves nor the substance of the subpoenas as required through separate statements. (See Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1345(c).) Plaintiff, in a late reply, requests the Court accept a curative separate statement. Given the other procedural deficiencies, this request is denied. 

 

Additionally, as argued by Defendants, Plaintiff did not meet and confer as required for her motion for a protective order. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 2025.420 [motion for protective order “shall be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under Section 2016.040.”].) Defendants state that other than the letter with Plaintiff’s objections, Plaintiff’s counsel did not make any contact with defense counsel. (Tetzlaff Decl., ¶ 5.) 

 

Finally, compounded by the issue that Plaintiff does not reveal how many deposition subpoenas are at issue, the deposition subpoenas may have had to be filed as separate motions. With multiple subpoenas at issue, and without knowledge of the type of deposition subpoenas, each one may have to be the subject of a separate motion with a separate filing fee and separate statement. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 2020.020, subd. (b); Gov. Code, § 70617, subds. (a), (f); Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1345(a)(5).) 

 

Accordingly, in light of the multiple procedural deficiencies, most importantly the failure to provide the deposition subpoenas or the text of the subpoenas, this motion is DENIED without prejudice on procedural grounds. 

Case Number: 25NWCV03015    Hearing Date: September 22, 2026    Dept: SEP

ABUJUBARA v. BMW OF NORTH AMERICA, LLC, ET AL. 

CASE NO.: 25NWCV03015 

HEARING:  09/22/2026 @ 10:30 AM 

 

#13 

TENTATIVE ORDER 

 

  1. Defendant BMW of North America, LLC’s motion for summary judgment is DENIED. 

 

  1. Defendant’s motion for summary adjudication as to the first and second causes of action is DENIED. 

 

Moving party to give notice.  

 

Defendant BMW of North America, LLC (BMW) moves for summary judgment, or alternatively summary adjudication of the first and second causes of action in the complaint. 

 

Background 

 

On August 21, 2025, Plaintiff Mesadaq Abujubara on behalf of Alfakir LLC (Plaintiff) filed this lemon law action against BMW, McKenna Motor Company, Inc. dba McKenna BMW, and Does 1 through 10. The complaint alleges that Plaintiff experienced defects and nonconformities to warranty with his 2021 BMW 5 Series, VIN: WBA53BH02MWX15746 (Subject Vehicle). (Complaint, ¶¶ 16-17.) The complaint asserts two causes of action: (1) violation of Song-Beverly Act – breach of express warranty against BMW and (2) negligent repair against McKenna Motor Company. 

 

Legal Standard 

 

The function of a motion for summary judgment or adjudication is to allow a determination as to whether an opposing party cannot show evidentiary support for a pleading or claim and to enable an order of summary dismissal without the need for trial. (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 843.) In reviewing a motion for summary judgment, courts apply a three-step analysis: “(1) identify the issues framed by the pleadings; (2) determine whether the moving party has negated the opponent’s claims; and (3) determine whether the opposition has demonstrated the existence of a triable, material factual issue.” (Hinesley v. Oakshade Town Center (2005) 135 Cal.App.4th 289, 294.) 

 

In moving for summary judgment, a defendant has the “burden of showing that a cause of action has no merit if the party has shown that one or more elements of the cause of action, even if not separately pleaded, cannot be established, or that there is a complete defense to the cause of action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (p)(2).) A defendant must support the motion “with evidence including ‘affidavits, declarations, admissions, answers to interrogatories, depositions, and matters of… judicial notice.’” (Aguilar, supra, 25 Cal.4th at p. 855, citing Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (b).) 

 

Once a moving party has satisfied the initial burden of proof, “the burden shifts to the plaintiff or cross-complainant to show that a triable issue of one or more material facts exists as to the cause of action or a defense thereto.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (p)(2).) To establish a triable issue of material fact, the party opposing the motion must produce substantial responsive evidence. (Sangster v. Paetkau (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 151, 166.) 

 

Summary judgment must be granted “if all the evidence submitted, and ‘all inferences reasonably deducible from the evidence’ and uncontradicted by other inferences or evidence, show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” (Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp. (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119, see also Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (c).) Courts “liberally construe the evidence in support of the party opposing summary judgment and resolve doubts concerning the evidence in favor of that party.” (Yanowitz v. L’Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1127.) 

 

Lodged Documents 

 

There appears to be confusion about whether certain documents should be filed under seal. As argued by Plaintiff, there are no protective orders or motions to seal on this record. 

 

Evidentiary Objections 

 

Plaintiff makes two evidentiary objections to the declaration of Marisa Moore. The Court rules as follows:  

 

OVERRULED: 1 

SUSTAINED: 2 

 

Plaintiff objects to Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 in the declaration of Marisa Moore on the grounds that Marisa Moore, as defense counsel, lacks personal knowledge and failed to authenticate the documents. For Exhibit 1, defense counsel attests: “Attached as Exhibit 1 is a true and correct copy of the Warranty Vehicle Inquiry that was produced to Plaintiff on November 12, 2025.” (Moore Decl., ¶ 2.) This is confirmed by the declaration of Plaintiff’s counsel. (Thomas Decl., ¶¶ 6-7.) The second objection does not state the same: “Attached as Exhibit 2 is a true and correct copy of the Motor Vehicle Retail Installment Sale Contract.” (Moore Decl., ¶ 3.) Submitting a declaration by counsel stating only that an attached copy is a “true and correct copy” is not sufficient to authenticate. (Claudio v. Regents of the University of California (2005) 134 Cal.App.4th 224, 244.) 

 

Discussion 

 

BMW moves for summary judgment or, alternatively, summary adjudication as to the first and second causes of action in the complaint. As the second cause of action is not alleged against BMW, the Court proceeds only as to the first cause of action. 

 

BMW moves on the grounds that the Subject Vehicle does not qualify as a “new motor vehicle” under the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act (Song-Beverly).  

 

BMW refers to the Supreme Court of California’s ruling in Rodriguez v. FCA US LLC [Rodriguez] (2024) 17 Cal.5th 189, 196. In Rodriguez, the Supreme Court considered whether a 2011 Dodge Ram 2500 which was bought used with an unexpired manufacturer’s warranty constituted a “new motor vehicle” and concluded that it “does not qualify as a ‘motor vehicle sold with a manufacturer's new car warranty’ under section 1793.22, subdivision (e)(2)’s definition of ‘new motor vehicle’ unless the new car warranty was issued with the sale.” (Id., at p. 196-97.) The Supreme Court of California held “that the phrase “other motor vehicle sold with a manufacturer's new car warranty” — considered in the context of the surrounding text of¿section 1793.22, subdivision (e)(2)¿and in the broader context of the Song-Beverly Act's provisions distinguishing between new and used goods — means a vehicle for which a manufacturer's¿new car warranty is issued with the sale.” (Id., at p. 206.) The Supreme Court reasoned that this distinction becomes apparent when looking at the exceptions for dealer-owned vehicles or demonstrators—“By specifically mentioning dealer-owned vehicles and demonstrators, the Legislature highlighted vehicles for which a manufacturer’s new car warranty arises upon sale to a retail buyer. Thus, the phrase ‘other motor vehicle sold with a manufacturer’s new car warranty’ is most naturally understood to mean other vehicles for which such a warranty is issued with the sale.” (Id., at p. 199-200.) 

 

BMW shows that the Subject Vehicle was originally sold with BMW’s 4-year/50,000 mile New Vehicle Limited Warranty which became effective on July 14, 2021. (UMF, ¶ 4.) It is undisputed that Plaintiff received the balance of that initial warranty with their purchase of the Subject Vehicle on June 26, 2024. (UMF, ¶ 4.) 

 

BMW argues that to the extent that Plaintiff argues that BMW issued a certified pre-owned (CPO) warranty to Plaintiff with the Subject Vehicle, a CPO warranty is not the same as a New Vehicle Limited Warranty. BMW argues that Rodriguez I, supra, 77 Cal.App.5th at p. 220 supports this view: “we think the most natural interpretation of the phrase ‘other motor vehicle sold with a manufacturer's new car warranty’ is that it, too, refers to vehicles that have never been previously sold to a consumer and come with full express warranties.”  

 

As such, BMW establishes that Plaintiff did not purchase the Subject Vehicle new, but rather purchased it used with a remaining balance of the New Vehicle Limited Warranty. Thus, BMW shifts the burden to Plaintiff.  

 

Plaintiff’s Opposition 

 

In opposition, Plaintiff points to the same Warranty Vehicle Inquiry produced by BMW to argue that it shows that a CPO warranty was effective as of July 14, 2021 with an enrollment date of June 26, 2024. (AMF, ¶ 11.) Plaintiff also refers to other documents produced by BMW including a document signed by BMW and Plaintiff stating “All BMW Certified vehicles … Are backed by the BMW Certified Warranty[.]” (AMF, ¶ 11.) 

 

Plaintiff argues that Rodriguez did not address whether a manufacturer who issued a CPO warranty for a used vehicle can be liable for a breach of express warranty claim under Civil Code section 1795.5. In Rodriguez, the Supreme Court noted “[f]or new products, liability extends to the manufacturer; for used products, liability extends to the distributor or retail seller and not to the manufacturer, at least where the manufacturer has not issued a new warranty or played a substantial role in the sale of a used good.” (Rodriguez, supra, 17 Cal.5th at p. 202.) Plaintiff argues that BMW’s arguments ignore Kiluk v. Mercedes-Benz USA, LLC [Kiluk] (2019) 43 Cal.App.5th 334 and that BMW failed to address this theory in the complaint. The complaint, which frames this motion, alleges “Defendant contracted to provide an additional warranty for the vehicle being certified pre-owned, which included additional coverage for the earlier of 12 Months (1 Year) or Unlimited Miles. Defendant stepped into the role of the retail seller by marketing its certified pre-owned warranty program and issuing a new express warranty at the time of sale.” (Complaint, ¶ 8.) 

 

Kiluk involved the sale of a CPO vehicle which was accompanied by an additional used vehicle warranty issued by the manufacturer in connection with the sale. (Id. at p. 336.) A jury found the defendant-manufacturer was liable under the SBA for breach of express and implied warranties. (Ibid.) The Court of Appeal affirmed this decision by concluding that “[a]lthough the Song-Beverly Act generally binds only distributors and retail sellers in the sale of used goods,…Mercedes Benz stepped into that role by issuing an express warranty on the sale of a used vehicle.” (Id., at p. 337.) The Court of Appeal reasoned:  

 

Mercedes Benz partnered with a dealership to sell used vehicles directly to the public by offering an express warranty as part of the sales package, which is a crucial incentive for buyers like plaintiff. By partnering with the dealership, Mercedes Benz stepped into the role of a retailer and was subject to the obligations of a retailer under¿section 1795.5. That section provides that a retailer's obligations are the “same” as a manufacturer under¿section 1793.2.¿ 

 

(Id., at p. 340.) The Kiluk Court noted that the parties disputed whether the subject vehicle was a “new motor vehicle” under the Song-Beverly Act but determined that “even if the vehicle was not a “new motor vehicle” under Song-Beverly Act, Mercedes Benz was still liable under the used goods provisions of¿section 1795.5.” (Ibid.) 

 

Here, the Court agrees with Plaintiff that even if BMW establishes that the Subject Vehicle was purchased used, there remains a triable issue as to whether BMW stepped into the shoes of a retailer by issuing the CPO warranty to Plaintiff and thus could be liable under Civil Code section 1795.5. 

 

BMW does not reply or address Kiluk. 

 

Accordingly, BMW’s motion for summary judgment and summary adjudication as to the first cause of action is DENIED. 

 

As noted above and raised by Plaintiff, the second cause of action for negligent repair is not asserted against BMW, and whether the Subject Vehicle is a used motor vehicle is not relevant to a negligent repair analysis. Therefore, BMW’s motion for summary adjudication as to the second cause of action is DENIED. 

 

  

Case Number: 26NWCV00324¿    Hearing Date: September 22, 2026    Dept: SEP

KIM v. ALASKA BENTO, INC. 

CASE NO.: 26NWCV00324¿  

HEARING: 09/22/2026 @ 9:30 AM 

 

#12 

TENTATIVE ORDER 

 

Defendant Alaska Bento Inc.’s motion to vacate default judgment and stay eviction is DENIED without prejudice.  

 

Moving party to give notice.  

 

Defendant Alaska Bento Inc. (Defendant) moves to vacate default judgment and stay an eviction. 

 

Background 

 

On January 27, 2026, Plaintiff Myung Hye Kim (Plaintiff) filed this unlawful detainer action against Defendant regarding the premises located at 5805 Florence Ave., Bell Gardens, CA 90201 (Premises). 

 

On March 27, 2026, Default was entered as to Defendant. On April 3, 2026, Default Judgment was entered for possession of the Premises. 

 

On April 6, 2026 a Writ of Possession was issued and on July 10, 2026, the Writ was returned. 

 

On September 15, 2026, Defendant filed a Substitution of Attorney reflecting that Defendant was formerly representing itself and is now represented by an attorney. 

 

Discussion 

 

On May 4, 2026, Defendant filed a Notice of Motion and Motion to Vacate Judgment and Request to Stay Eviction. 

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that Defendant cannot represent itself as a corporation. 

 

Merco Constr. Engineers, Inc. v. Municipal Court (1978) 21 Cal.3d 724, 730, provides the long-standing rule that “[a] corporation cannot represent itself in court, either in propria persona or through an officer or agent who is not an attorney.” The rule has since been relaxed such that there is an “increasing acceptance of the view that representation of the corporation by an attorney is not an absolute prerequisite to the court's fundamental power to hear or determine a case,…it is more appropriate and just to treat a corporation's failure to be represented by an attorney as a defect that may be corrected, on such terms as are just in the sound discretion of the court.” (CLD Construction, Inc. v. City of San Ramon (2004) 120 Cal.App.4th 1141, 1149.) 

 

Here, since the instant motion was brought by Defendant while Defendant was not represented, the Court cannot rule on or grant this motion. However, in light of the shifting perspective that representation is a defect that may be corrected and that Defendant has taken steps to correct this defect, Defendant is not precluded from filing a motion for the relief requested here after curing this defect.  

 

Accordingly, Defendant’s motion to vacate default judgment and stay the eviction is DENIED without prejudice.
